https://www.politico.eu/article/romania-.text: Romania’s center-left opposition must urgently decide whether to support a new pro-European government or be blamed for the far right gaining control, warned the country’s potential next prime minister. In an interview with POLITICO, European lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan said he would ask the Social Democratic Party (PSD) to back his center-right National Liberal Party (PNL) in a new vote “by the end of next week,” even though the PSD’s leadership has so far refused to do so. “Romanian socialists are facing a moment of truth — they need to decide whether they behave as responsible European social democrats and support a pro-European government or whether they are intensifying their cooperation with the radical right, the anti-European populistic extremist party here,” said Mureșan, who is the third person tasked with forming a government since the ruling coalition lost a no-confidence vote in May. Advertisement Advertisement Another failure in Bucharest would set up a divisive early election in the EU’s seventh-most-populous country, where the far right is leading the polls at a moment when populist-nationalist parties are surging in countries around Europe. Mainstream parties in Romania — a key strategic NATO ally that has suffered some spillover from Russia’s war in Ukraine — have barely fought off the far right in a series of parliamentary and presidential elections that began in winter 2024. PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu said on Monday that the group will not vote in favor of Mureșan’s government and would only support the formation of a government it forms part of. He has not, however, closed the door to a coalition with the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), which has courted confrontation with Brussels and supported pro-Russian candidates. The PSD and AUR voted together to bring down the previous government earlier this year. Mureșan called on the EU’s center-left S&D group leadership in Brussels to prevent that from happening, arguing they “are obviously responsible for what their member parties are doing” and arguing they “will have a very significant problem of credibility, shall they continue to be silent about their Romanian members partner cooperating closely with the far right.” “As long as the European socialists are not acting to prevent this in a very credible way from happening, we cannot exclude socialists in other countries going this way, unfortunately, as well,” he added. Grindeanu, however, has suggested that his PSD could be convinced to enter discussions with Mureșan if he agrees to include ten policy proposals identified as core for the PSD. Among them are a new push for energy infrastructure, a defense and national security uplift, public services reform and investment in education and healthcare. Advertisement Advertisement However, if the proposed cabinet and policy program is rejected, President Nicușor Dan will gain the constitutional power to order new elections — the first since 2024, when the AUR made major gains and became the second-largest party in parliament. Mureșan acknowledged that the far-right faction is now polling at around 35 percent, compared to just 21 percent for his own center-right PNL. “Early elections are not my preferred option,” said Mureșan. “I believe that we should try to form a pro-European government now. But should this not be possible, I think they should not be ruled out.” The request from Dan, who last year beat the AUR’s controversial candidate George Simion in the race for the presidency, comes at an awkward time for Mureșan. Currently serving as a member of the European Parliament, he is one of the chief negotiators on the EU’s €2 trillion long-term budget, which the bloc’s leaders want to see finalized by the end of the year. According to him, though, the far right taking control of Romania would make that job far harder because “any anti-European government around the table would want Europe to be weaker. They know that the budget is an important tool to keep Europe strong, and they would basically vote against an ambitious and realistic [budget].” On top of that, “we would have a government which would be very friendly to Russia, and all of this would be bad for the people of Romania, for the European Union.” Tim Ross and Max Griera contributed reporting. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Oleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain. Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine Brigade View image in fullscreen Oleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain. Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine Brigade Ukraine ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones Peter Beaumont and Artem Mazhulin Sun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages. “We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces. Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.” Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there. This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians. The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted. The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday. In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”. He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.” Russian occupation of Ukraine The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents. Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted. Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save. In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed. “We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.” On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops. Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested. Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far. “Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation. “Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.” He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.” View image in fullscreen War-damaged buildings in Oleshky. Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine Brigade According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult. “The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult. “And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.” Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers. “Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said. Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack. Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.” She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.” In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.” Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic. “They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says Trains carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.baltictimes.com/kulbergs_cal.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Kulbergs calls for issue of Istanbul Convention to be put to a consultative referendum 2026-10-07 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Public opinion on the Istanbul Convention could be gauged through a consultative referendum, the results of which would not be legally binding, Prime Minister and future candidate for the office, Andris Kulbergs (United List), said in a conversation with members of the press on Wednesday following a meeting with President Edgars Rinkevics. Kulbergs stated that the United List had discussed the idea of a consultative referendum with the President. In his view, the Saeima could use such a referendum to pose a question to the public, receive an answer, and act accordingly. The politician noted that the issue of the Istanbul Convention has generated significant public interest, making it a suitable topic for gauging public opinion in this way. Other questions could also be posed in consultative referendums. Although the results would not be legally binding, they would provide a clear signal to political forces and eliminate speculation, Kulbergs believes. When asked whether postponing withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention is a condition for forming a new government, Kulbergs denied this. He emphasized that the public has given the United List a mandate for change, not for addressing ideological and divisive issues, so such matters are not on the United List’s agenda. "Whether we will at some point hold a consultative poll or a referendum, and what politicians should do afterward, that is an open question," added Rinkevics, while noting that introducing a consultative referendum would first require changes to the law, which would take time. The President added that there are differing opinions among legal experts regarding the possibility of putting international treaties to a referendum. While working on this issue last year, a large number of legal experts pointed to the possibility of putting a bill to denounce a convention to a referendum - rather than the treaty itself - while others held the opposite view. Rinkevics emphasized that he currently sees no argument why Latvia should rush to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention, thereby becoming the first European Union (EU) country to take such a step. The President reminded that, when submitting the bill to the Saeima for a second review, he had called for the issue to be left to the next parliamentary session and discussed in pre-election debates. The positions of the political parties have varied - some supported remaining in the convention, some strongly advocated for withdrawal, while others were willing to consider various options. In his view, this is not an issue that needs to be rushed. Rinkevics noted that the new Saeima and government will face many pressing issues that require immediate attention. In consultations with most of the parties, he heard a willingness not to lower human rights standards or to raise issues that divide society. As reported, last fall the United List, then in the opposition, together with other political forces, pushed for Latvia’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention, and the Saeima supported it, but the proposal sparked widespread public protests. President Edgars Rinkevics did not promulgate the law and referred it back to parliament for further review. The Saeima essentially agreed to entrust the final decision on the matter to the next parliamentary session, in which the United List has now gained a dominant role. The United List's candidate for Prime Minister, current Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs - whom the President would like to see form the next government as well - has promised to focus his efforts on putting the country’s finances in order, ensuring security, and promoting economic growth. The President expressed his view that, in his opinion, this issue should not be raised at this time. He would support the position of allowing the new Saeima and the Cabinet of Ministers to settle into their roles, while acknowledging that the issue of the convention might resolve itself. Rinkevics also noted that the Saeima had adopted a resolution to draft a special law that would incorporate the positive aspects of the Istanbul Convention, but the government has yet to implement this resolution. As another option under consideration, the President mentioned keeping the convention in force while simultaneously initiating discussions with Council of Europe (CoE) member states to clarify the provisions open to interpretation. He acknowledged that this would take a long time and emphasized that the issue should be resolved in a way that does not divide society.
